title: Redundant Edge
statement:
A connected network of n nodes was built as a tree and then given one extra edge; find the edge that should be removed.

Contract
- Nodes are labelled `1` to `n`, and `edges` holds exactly `n` pairs `{a, b}` in the order they were added. Without the extra edge the graph would be a tree, so it is connected.
- The extra edge may repeat an existing pair or be a self-loop (`a == b`).
- Return the edge that, once removed, leaves a tree. When several edges qualify (every edge on the single cycle does), return the one that appears last in `edges`.
- Return the pair exactly as it appears in the input, as a new array. Do not modify `edges`.

Examples
- `redundantEdge(new int[][]{{4,1},{2,3},{1,2},{3,4}})` returns `[3, 4]`: all four edges lie on the cycle and `[3, 4]` comes last.
- `redundantEdge(new int[][]{{1,2},{2,3},{3,4},{4,1},{5,1}})` returns `[4, 1]`, not the final edge, which is a harmless branch.
- `redundantEdge(new int[][]{{2,1},{1,2}})` returns `[1, 2]`.
hints: Adding edges one at a time keeps the graph a forest until an edge joins two nodes that were already connected.
Keep a disjoint-set (union-find) structure over the nodes. For each edge in order, find both endpoints' roots; if they match, this edge closes the cycle.

The first edge whose endpoints are already connected is the last cycle edge in input order. Use path compression so the find steps stay cheap. Intended complexity: O(n) time (near-linear with path compression) and O(n) space for the parent array, where n is the number of nodes.
inputSyntax: Input: the edge list as nested [a, b] pairs, for example: [[4, 1], [2, 3], [1, 2], [3, 4]]
